0.s: Which one of the following is a reason why astronomical distances are measured in light-years?

0.x: For most space objects, we use light-years to describe their distance. A light-year is the distance light travels in one Earth year. One light-year is about 6 trillion miles (9 trillion km). The reason why astronomical distances are measured in light-years is because the speed of light is constant and very high. Light travels at a speed of approximately 299,792 kilometers per second General Science PMF IAS S&T – 40 (186,282 miles per second) in a vacuum. This speed is so immense that when we talk about the vast distances in space, using common units like kilometers or miles becomes impractical. Since the speed of light is same, if we know the time it takes for light to travel a certain distance, we can easily calculate that distance in terms of light-years.

White dwarf stars, which are remnants of stars that have exhausted their nuclear fuel, exhibit extreme densities that challenge conventional understandings of stellar behaviour. Chandrasekhar's calculations demonstrated that for white dwarfs exceeding this mass limit, electron degeneracy pressure—a quantum-mechanical effect that prevents further collapse—would be insufficient to counteract gravitational forces, leading to continued contraction.

0.x: The detection of microwaves in space is correct: With a traditional optical telescope, the space between stars and galaxies is completely dark. However, a sensitive radio telescope shows a faint background glow. This glow is strongest in the microwave region of the radio spectrum and is therefore called the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB). CMB, also known as relic radiation (thermal radiation left over from the "Big Bang"), is fundamental to observational cosmology because it is the oldest light in the Universe and can be found in all directions. Its discovery is considered a landmark proof for the concept of "accelerating expansion of the universe" and the Big Bang Theory. Observation of the redshift phenomenon in space is correct: Redshift and Blueshift describe how light changes as objects in space (such as stars or galaxies) move closer or farther away from us. American astronomer Edwin Hubble was the first to describe the redshift phenomenon (galactic redshift) and tie it to an expanding universe (galaxies are drifting apart). 1.s: If the earth's direction of rotation is reversed, what would be the IST when it is noon at the International Date Line?
1.x: Normally, the Earth rotates from west to east, so places in the east are ahead in time. IST (82.5° E) is therefore 6 hours 30 minutes behind the International Date Line (180°). If the Earth's direction of rotation were reversed, time calculation would also reverse, and places to the west would become ahead in time. Since IST lies west of the Physical Geography PMF IAS Geo – 39 International Date Line by 97.5° longitude, IST would be 6 hours 30 minutes ahead of it. Therefore, when it is 12:00 noon at the International Date Line, IST would be 18:30 hrs (6:30 PM).

1.s: When there is noon at G.M.T. meridian, people at another place on the Earth are taking their 6 o'clock morning tea. The longitude of the place is
1.x: When it is 12:00 noon at the Greenwich meridian (GMT), a place that is 6 hours behind will show 6:00 AM. Since the Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, it covers 15° of longitude per hour (or 1° in 4 minutes). Thus, a 1-hour time difference equals 15° of longitude. A 6-hour difference corresponds to 6 × 15° = 90°. Because the local time is earlier than GMT, the location lies to the west of Greenwich — at 90° W longitude.

1.s: The local time of a place is 6:00 AM when the Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) is 3:00 AM, what is the longitude of the place ?
1.x: Greenwich Mean Time (G.M.T.) is referred to as Coordinated Universal Time (U.T.C.). International time is calculated from Greenwich at the 0 Meridian, and the time eastward of it is while the time westward of it is behind (although dates are measured from the 1800 meridian at the International Date Line which passes through the mid of the Pacific Ocean). Meridians situated 1800 east of Greenwich are called East-meridians and meridians situated at 1800 west are known as West-meridians. All the meridians in 3600 of the globe are divided into 24 time zones (150 – 150 meridian difference). Therefore, each time zone has a 1 hour time difference and each meridian has the difference of 4 minutes, moving each meridian east G.M.T. time is 4 minutes ahead and moving west of G.M.T. time remains 4 minutes behind for each meridian. According to the question time is to be calculated for that place which is ahead (6-3=3 hrs) of Greenwich. As we know for 1 hours difference in longitude (meridian) is 150 therefore for 3 hours the difference will be 15 × 3 = 450 , So that place will lie at 450 east of Greenwich.

direction keeping the polestar to his right
1.x: A pole star is a star or a star system situated in the direction of the earth's axis. At present, Polaris or North Star (a system of 3 stars) is the earth's pole star. The Northern Hemisphere has its shortest night during the June solstice. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
The North Pole is tilted toward the Sun during the June solstice. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
The Equator has approximately a 12-hour day during the June solstice. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
The Northern Hemisphere has its longest day on 21 June. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
xa: At the June solstice the Sun is overhead at the **Tropic of Cancer** (**23.5°N**).
At the **December solstice** the **South Pole** tilts toward the Sun and the Antarctic has continuous daylight.
**Tropic of Cancer** day length on **21 June:** ~**13½ h**.

1.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: 21 March – Sun overhead at the Equator, moving northward
21/22 December – Sun overhead at the Tropic of Cancer
21 June – Sun overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, starting to move southward
23 September – Sun overhead at the Equator, moving southward
1.x: On 21/22 December the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn, not Cancer.
n: On 21 March, the Sun is overhead at the Equator. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
On 21 March, the Sun starts moving northward after being overhead at the Equator. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
On 21 June, the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
On 21 June, the Sun starts moving southward after being overhead at the Tropic of Cancer. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
On 23 September, the Sun is overhead at the Equator. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
After 23 September, the Sun continues moving southward. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
On 21 or 22 December, the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
xa: **21 March:** spring begins in the **Northern Hemisphere**, autumn in the **Southern**.
**21 June:** NH **summer**, **longest day**; SH **winter**.
**22 December:** SH **summer**, **longest day**.

1.s: During the summer season in the Southern Hemisphere, which pole is tilted towards the Sun?
1.x: During southern summer, the South Pole is tilted towards the Sun, producing longer days and summer conditions in the Southern Hemisphere.
1.tq: Relate the hemisphere experiencing summer to the direction of axial tilt.
xs: During the Southern Hemisphere's summer, the **South Pole** is tilted towards the Sun — option **(1)**.
Seasons come from the **tilted axis** plus **revolution**: the hemisphere tilted toward the Sun gets summer.
The **North Pole** tilts toward the Sun in the Northern summer (**21 June** solstice), so it cannot be the answer.
xa: On **22 December** the Sun is overhead at the **Tropic of Capricorn** — the **Southern Hemisphere's longest day** and summer.
The North Pole is **continuously lit from ~21 March to ~23 September**; the **South Pole** in the other half-year.
Earth's orbit is **elliptical**; revolution takes **365¼ days**, so every 4th year is a **leap year** (29 Feb).

1.s: When the North Pole has six months of continuous daylight, what does the South Pole have?
1.x: Axial inclination and revolution give the poles opposite six-month patterns of day and night.
n: The North Pole has six months of continuous daylight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The North Pole has six months of darkness. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The South Pole has the opposite daylight and darkness pattern to the North Pole. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The main reason for polar six-month day and night is axial inclination combined with revolution. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
xa: North Pole is continuously lit from ~**21 March** to ~**23 September**.
**Arctic Circle:** **24 h day** on **21 June**, **24 h night** on **22 Dec**.
Continuous daylight occurs **beyond the Antarctic Circle** during **Southern Hemisphere summer**.

1.s: What does the Arctic Circle experience on 22 December?
1.x: On 22 December the Arctic Circle has 24 hours of night; on 21 June it has 24 hours of day.

1.s: What is the period from 22 December to 21 June, when the Sun appears to move northward, called?
1.x: Uttarayana is the Sun's apparent northward movement from 22 December to 21 June.

1.s: Which of the following cities has the shortest day on 21 June?
1.x: On 21 June day length grows northward, so the southernmost city, Thiruvananthapuram, has the shortest day.

2.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about sources of information on the Earth's interior?
o: Magma and lava from volcanic eruptions give direct evidence
Meteorites are used because they are made of material similar to the Earth's
Meteorites provide direct evidence of the interior
2.x: Meteorites are an indirect source; only material such as magma and lava gives direct evidence.
xa: **Seismic waves** are the **most important** indirect source.
Rise of **pressure and temperature with depth** is also indirect evidence.
Direct sources also include **deep drilling** and **surface rock from mining**.

2.s: On which peninsula did the USSR drill the deepest hole, about 12 km deep, in the 1970s?
2.x: The ~12 km hole was drilled on the Kola Peninsula; the Mponeng and TauTona mines (South Africa) reach only about 3.9 km.
xa: ⚠ Deepest hole = **Kola** (~12 km); deepest mines = **Mponeng, TauTona** (3.9 km).
India's scientific deep drilling: **Borehole Geophysics Research Laboratory, Karad**.
Direct sources: mining, drilling, **volcanic eruptions**.

2.s: Which one of the following gives indirect evidence about the Earth's interior?
2.x: Meteorites are an indirect source; mining rock, lava and drilling are direct sources.
2.tq: one-liner

2.s: In which country are Mponeng and TauTona, the deepest mines (about 3.9 km)?
2.x: Mponeng and TauTona are in South Africa; the Kola deep hole (~12 km) is in the former USSR.
2.tq: one-liner

2.s: Which one of the following is a direct source of information about the interior of the Earth?
2.x: Surface rocks obtained from mining areas are a direct source because the material itself is examined. Seismic waves, gravity anomalies and magnetic surveys are indirect sources that infer the interior from measurements.
2.tq: Mining, drilling, volcanoes = direct; seismic, gravity, magnetic, meteorites = indirect.
xs: **Surface rocks from mining areas** are a direct source — option **(3)**.
**Seismic waves**, **gravity** anomalies and **magnetic** surveys are all **indirect** sources.
This was the APPSC-G1 **2017** answer.
xa: Other direct sources: **deep drilling** and **volcanic eruptions** (magma, lava).
**Seismic waves** are the **most important** indirect source.
Deepest mines: **Mponeng, TauTona** (South Africa), only **3.9 km**.

2.s: The tremors produce waves on the surface of the earth which are called seismic waves. They are recorded by an instrument called the seismograph which is a:

2.s: During an earthquake, which type of waves get generated?
2.x: The seismic waves are generated in three forms. (1) P- (Primary) Waves – these waves travel fastest. (2) S - (Secondary) Wavesthese waves cause particles to oscillate. Both P and S waves are called ‘Body waves’ because they can travel through the interior of the Earth. (3) Surface Waves – these waves arrive after P and S waves and are confined to the surface of the Earth during an earthquake. There are two types of surface waves (i) Love waves and (ii) Rayleigh waves. 3. Read the following statement related to 'Earthquake shadow zone' and choose the correct option: Statement I : The shadow zone of one earthquake is totally different from the shadow zone of another earthquake Statement II : Seismometers record both 'P' and 'S' waves at any distance out of 105º from earthquake's epicentre (a) Statement I and Statement II both are true (b) Statement I is true, but Statement II is false (c) Statement I is false, but Statement II is true (d) Statement I and Statement II both are false Chhattisgarh P.C.S. (Pre) 2020 Ans. (b) Earthquake waves get recorded in seismographs. However, there exist some specific areas where the waves are not reported. Such a zone is called the 'Shadowzone'. The study of different events reveals that for each earthquake, there exists an altogether different shadow zone. P waves don't arrive between 1050 (1030 - 1050) and 1400 due to refraction at the mantle-core boundary, however S waves don't reappear beyond an angular distance of ~ 1300 as they are stopp

2.s: What are surface seismic waves also called?
2.x: Surface waves are L-waves; P-waves are primary and S-waves secondary waves.
n: P-waves are primary waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
S-waves are secondary waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
P-waves are also called compressional or longitudinal waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Surface waves are also called L-waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: P-waves **arrive first**; surface waves **arrive last**.
Surface waves do the **most damage**.
**National Centre for Seismology** (MoES): **160-observatory** network, detects Indian quakes of M **3.0+**.

2.s: What is the nature of P-waves?
2.x: In P-waves particles vibrate parallel to propagation (push–pull); in S-waves they vibrate perpendicular (transverse).
n: P-wave particle vibration is parallel to the direction of propagation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
S-wave particle vibration is perpendicular to the direction of propagation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
P-waves are longitudinal push-pull waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
S-waves are transverse shake waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: P-waves travel through **solids, liquids and gases**; S-waves through **solids only**.
P-waves are the **fastest**; **surface waves** the **slowest**.
**Velocity changes** and **shadow zones** reveal internal boundaries.

2.s: Beyond about how many degrees from the epicentre are S-waves absent everywhere?
2.x: S-waves are absent beyond 105°, so the S-wave shadow zone is larger than the P-wave shadow zone.
xa: CGPSC **2020** keyed the "own shadow zone" statement as true.
The S-wave shadow proves the **outer core is liquid**.
⚠ P = solids + liquids + gases; S = **solids only**.

2.s: Which of the following statements about seismic waves is incorrect?
o: S-waves can travel through solids and liquids.
P-waves are the fastest seismic waves and arrive first.
S-waves are transverse or shear waves.
Surface waves have the highest destructive power.
2.x: Option A is incorrect: S-waves travel only through solids and stop at liquids. P-waves arrive first, S-waves are shear waves and surface waves do most damage.
2.tq: Check the medium each wave can cross.
n: S-waves are also called transverse or shear waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
P-waves are the fastest seismic waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
P-waves arrive first. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
S-waves travel through solids. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
S-waves do not travel through liquids. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Surface waves have the highest destructive power. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
S-waves travel through solids only. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xs: The incorrect statement is "**S-waves can travel through solids and liquids**" — option **(1)**: S-waves pass through **solids only**.
The others are correct: **P-waves** are the **fastest** and **arrive first**; **S-waves** are **transverse or shear**; **surface waves** are the **most destructive**.
xa: P-waves pass through **solids, liquids and gases**.
P-waves reach the inner core at **11.23 km/s**.
**Surface waves** (L-waves) are the **slowest** and do **not** travel through the interior.
⚠ P = solids + liquids + gases; S = **solids only**.

2.s: S-waves disappear on reaching the outer core. In what state is the outer core?
2.x: S-waves cannot pass through liquids, so they vanish at the liquid outer core.
n: The outer core is liquid. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
S-waves stop in the outer core. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
S-waves disappear because the outer core is liquid. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
S-waves do not travel through liquids. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
S-waves travel through solids only. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]

2.s: Between which angular distances does the P-wave shadow zone approximately lie?
2.x: P-waves are strongly refracted at the mantle–core boundary, so they are not recorded about 105°–145° from the epicentre (often given as 103°–142°). Of the options, 103° and 142° is the only one that matches this zone.
n: P-waves are the fastest seismic waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
S-waves do not travel through liquids. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Surface waves have the highest destructive power. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The standard P-wave shadow zone is approximately 103°–142°. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
S-waves travel through solids only. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]

2.s: Why do seismic waves help in identifying discontinuities inside the Earth?
o: Their speed remains constant in all materials.
They are produced only by volcanic eruptions.
They travel only through the crust and stop at the Moho.
Their speed changes with density, causing reflection and refraction at layer boundaries.
2.x: Changes in density alter seismic-wave velocity and produce reflection and refraction at boundaries, revealing internal discontinuities.
2.tq: Connect the observable wave effect with the inferred internal structure.
xs: Wave **speed changes with density**, so waves **reflect and refract** at layer boundaries — option **(4)**.
That is how the **discontinuities** were found; speed is not constant (option 1).
P-waves cross the core, so waves do not stop at the **Moho** (option 3).
xa: At the **Moho**, P-wave speed jumps from **6.9** to **8.1 km/s**.
Downward order: **Conrad → Moho → Repetti → Gutenberg → Lehmann**.
**Seismic waves** are the **most important** indirect source.

2.s:
Consider the following statements about seismic shadow zones:
1. Each earthquake has its own shadow zone, set by its epicentre.
2. The S-wave shadow zone is smaller than the P-wave shadow zone.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
2.x: Each earthquake has its own shadow zone. S-waves are absent beyond 105°, so their shadow is bigger, not smaller.
2.tq: statements

2.s: Which seismic waves cause the most damage?
2.x: Surface (L) waves are the slowest but cause the highest damage.
2.tq: one-liner

2.s: Which instrument records seismic waves?
2.x: P, S and surface waves are recorded by the seismograph.

2.s: Unlike the fluid core of the Earth, the core of the moon is–
2.x: The fluid core of the Earth while the core of the moon is solid.

2.s: Which layer lies directly below the mantle?
2.x: The crust is outermost, then the mantle, then the outer core, with the inner core at the centre.
n: Earth’s crust is the outermost layer. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The mantle lies below the crust. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The outer core lies below the mantle. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The inner core is central. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: **Crust:** oxygen is the **most abundant** element.
**Outer core** is **liquid** (**2,900–5,150 km**); **inner core** **solid** (**5,150–6,371 km**).
**Moho** separates crust and mantle; **Lehmann** separates outer and inner core.

2.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the approximate thickness of oceanic and continental crust respectively?
2.x: Oceanic crust is approximately 5 km thick, whereas continental crust is approximately 30 km thick, though it may reach greater thickness beneath mountains.
2.tq: Use the direct numerical comparison and distinguish oceanic from continental crust.
xs: Oceanic crust is **~5 km**, continental crust **~30 km** — option **(2)**.
Continental crust reaches **~70 km** under **mountains**.
Some notes give a mean of **~20 km** — neither option (1) nor (4) matches the oceanic/continental pair.
xa: Continental crust is **granitic (SIAL)**; oceanic is **basaltic (SIMA)**.
Crust density: upper **2.8**, lower **3.0**.
The **Moho** lies **~30 km** under continents and **~5 km** under oceans.

2.s: The mantle accounts for approximately what percentage of the Earth's volume and mass respectively?
2.x: The mantle constitutes approximately 83% of Earth's volume and 68% of its mass.
2.tq: Distinguish the volume share from the mass share rather than reversing them.
xs: The mantle is **83%** of Earth's volume and **68%** of its mass — option **(1)**.
**16%** and **32%** are the **core's** volume and mass shares — option (2) is the trap.
xa: ⚠ Mantle = **83%** volume, **68%** mass; core = **16%** volume, **32%** mass.
Mantle extends from the Moho to **2,900 km**; mean density **4.6**.

2.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Earth's core?
o: The outer core extends from about 2,900 km to 5,150 km
The inner core extends from about 5,150 km to the centre at 6,371 km
2.x: The inner core is solid; only the outer core is liquid.
xa: Inner-core density **13.3-13.6**; P-waves cross at **11.23 km/s**.
**Gutenberg** (~**2,900 km**) and **Lehmann** (~**5,150 km**) mark these boundaries.
Core = **16%** of volume, **32%** of mass.

2.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the approximate density progression from the crust through the mantle to the inner core?
2.x: Density increases downward from approximately 2.8–3.0 g/cm³ in the crust to 4.6 in the mantle and 13.3–13.6 in the inner core.
2.tq: Arrange the density values in increasing order with depth.
xs: Density goes **2.8-3.0 (crust) → 4.6 (mantle) → 13.3-13.6 (inner core)** — option **(2)**.
**5.5** is Earth's **average**, not the mantle's (options 1 and 4 wrong).
Option (3) reverses the order.
xa: Outer core density **~10-12**.
Upper crust **2.8**, lower crust **3.0**.
Density rises with depth, along with **temperature** and **pressure**.

2.s: Which layer of the Earth is predominantly solid but behaves plastically over geological time?
2.x: The mantle is mostly solid but flows slowly over geological time, which drives convection. The outer core is liquid and the crust and inner core are rigid.
2.tq: Discriminate the state of each layer.
n: The mantle is predominantly solid. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The mantle behaves plastically over geological time. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xs: The **mantle** is **predominantly solid** but **behaves plastically over geological time** — option **(1)**.
The **crust** is **solid**; the **outer core** is **liquid**; the **inner core** is **solid** (the **NIFE** or **solid core**).
The mantle is mainly **magnesium–iron silicates**, extending from the Moho to **2,900 km**.
xa: Mantle = **83%** of volume, **68%** of mass; mean density **4.6**.
**Mantle movement drives plate movement**; the mantle is the **major source region for magma**.

2.s: What type of rock is oceanic crust mainly made of?
2.x: Oceanic crust is basaltic, denser and richer in Fe–Mg, while continental crust is thicker and generally older.
n: Continental crust is thicker than oceanic crust. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Basalt is the main rock of oceanic crust. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Oceanic crust has higher density than continental crust. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Continental crust is generally older than oceanic crust. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Oceanic crust contains more iron and magnesium. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: Continental crust is **granitic (SIAL)**; oceanic **basaltic (SIMA)**.
Thickness: oceanic ~**5 km**, continental ~**30 km**, up to ~**70 km** under mountains.
Crust density: upper **2.8**, lower **3.0**.

2.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Outer core – Contains liquid iron and nickel
Inner core – Lies just below the crust
Core – Begins at about 660 km depth
2.x: The outer core contains liquid iron and nickel. The mantle lies below the crust, the inner core is solid iron and the core begins at about 2,900 km.
n: The mantle lies below the crust. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
The outer core consists of liquid iron and nickel. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
The inner core consists of solid iron. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
Earth’s core begins at a depth of 2,900 km. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
xa: **Proof** of the liquid outer core: **loss of S-waves**.
Inner core density **13.3–13.6**; it stays solid under **immense pressure**.
Core share: **16%** of Earth's volume, **32%** of its mass.
The **Gutenberg** discontinuity (~**2,900 km**) separates mantle and outer core.

2.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Compositional layering of the Earth consists of the crust, mantle and core.
2. Mechanical layering of the Earth consists only of the crust, mantle and core.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
2.x: By composition Earth has crust, mantle and core; mechanical layers are lithosphere, asthenosphere, mesosphere, outer core and inner core, so statement 2 is wrong.
n: Compositional layering consists of the crust, mantle, and core. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Mechanical layering consists of the lithosphere, asthenosphere, deeper mantle, outer core, and inner core. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: **Lithosphere** = crust + uppermost mantle, about **100 km** thick, **rigid**.
**Asthenosphere** = weak, ductile **low-velocity zone** at ~**100–200 km**.
Layer sequence: Lithosphere → Asthenosphere → Mesosphere → **Barysphere (core)**.

2.s: Why does the inner core remain solid despite the very high temperature prevailing there?
o: Its temperature is lower than that of the crust.
The pressure exerted by the overlying rocks is immense.
It is located outside the mantle.
2.x: The immense pressure caused by the weight of overlying material keeps the inner core solid despite its extreme temperature.
2.tq: Link the physical condition to the controlling factor rather than to temperature alone.
xs: The **immense pressure** of overlying rock keeps the inner core solid — option **(2)**.
Pressure rises with the **weight of overlying rock**.
The inner core is not cooler than the crust — temperature **rises with depth**.
xa: ⚠ Outer core **liquid**, inner core **solid** (pressure).
Core main elements: **iron and nickel** — so option (4) is wrong.

2.s: Down to about what depth does the mantle extend from the Moho?
2.x: The mantle runs from the Moho to about 2,900 km, where the core begins.
2.tq: one-liner

2.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the continental crust?
o: It is thicker than the oceanic crust
It is older than the oceanic crust
2.x: Continental crust is thicker, older and granitic; basaltic rock marks the oceanic crust.
2.tq: NOT

2.s: The core constitutes approximately what percentage of the Earth's volume and mass respectively?
2.x: The core accounts for approximately 16% of Earth's volume and 32% of its mass.
2.tq: Distinguish the core's volume share from its greater mass share.
xs: The core is **16%** of Earth's volume and **32%** of its mass — option **(1)**.
**83%** and **68%** are the **mantle's** shares — option (4) is the trap.
xa: Core main elements: **iron and nickel (NIFE)**.
Core density **11-13.6** (inner core **13+**).
The core begins at **~2,900 km**.

2.s: What is the approximate rise in the velocity of P-waves at the Mohorovicic Discontinuity?
2.x: A distinctive increase in P-wave velocity from about 6.9 to 8.1 km/s helped identify the Moho.
2.tq: Recall the paired numerical values associated with a seismic boundary.
xs: At the **Moho**, P-wave speed jumps from **6.9 to 8.1 km/s** — option **(4)**.
**11.23 km/s** is the P-wave speed at the **inner core**.
xa: The Moho separates **crust and mantle**; found **1909**.
Wave **speed changes with density**, so waves **reflect and refract** at boundaries.
Moho depth: **~30 km** under continents, **~5 km** under oceans.

2.s: In which year was the Mohorovicic Discontinuity, separating the crust from the mantle, discovered?
2.x: Andrija Mohorovicic identified it in 1909; it lies about 30 km below continents and 5 km below oceans.
xa: At the Moho, P-wave speed jumps from **6.9** to **8.1 km/s**.
Rare **continental mantle earthquakes** occur **80+ km** below the Moho.
**Conrad** lies above it, within the crust.

2.s: Which of the following pairs (discontinuity – position counted from the Earth's surface) is correctly matched?
2.x: From the surface downward the discontinuities are Conrad (upper/lower crust), Mohorovicic (crust/mantle), Repetti (upper/lower mantle), Gutenberg (mantle/outer core) and Lehmann (outer/inner core). So Conrad is first; Mohorovicic is second, not fourth, and Gutenberg and Lehmann lie much deeper.

2.s: Which layers does the Gutenberg discontinuity separate?
2.x: Gutenberg separates mantle and outer core; Moho, crust and mantle; Lehmann, outer and inner core; Conrad, upper and lower crust.
n: The Mohorovicic or Moho discontinuity separates the crust and mantle. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The Gutenberg discontinuity separates the mantle and outer core. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The Lehmann discontinuity separates the outer core and inner core. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The Conrad discontinuity separates the upper and lower continental crust. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: At the **Moho**, P-wave speed jumps from **6.9** to **8.1 km/s**; found by **Andrija Mohorovicic** in **1909**.
**Repetti** separates upper and lower mantle (~**700–1,000 km**).
**Gutenberg** ~**2,900 km**; **Lehmann** ~**5,150 km**.
⚠ The most confused trio: **Moho**, **Gutenberg**, **Lehmann**.

2.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The 410 km and 660 km discontinuities mark mineralogical zones in the mantle.
2. Phase changes are associated with the 410 km and 660 km mantle zones.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
2.x: Both are true: the 410 km and 660 km discontinuities mark mineral phase changes in the mantle.
n: The 410 km and 660 km discontinuities mark mantle mineralogical zones. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Phase changes occur at the 410 km and 660 km mantle discontinuities. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: **Repetti** discontinuity separates upper and lower mantle (~**700–1,000 km**).
Old scheme: upper mantle to **1,000 km**, lower mantle **1,000–2,900 km**.

2.s: Which layers does the Conrad discontinuity separate?
2.x: The Conrad discontinuity lies between the upper and lower crust (SIAL and SIMA).
2.tq: one-liner

2.s: Which discontinuity separates the outer core from the inner core?
2.x: The Lehmann discontinuity (~5,150 km) separates the outer and inner core; Gutenberg separates the mantle and outer core.
2.tq: one-liner

2.s: Which layers does the Repetti discontinuity separate?
2.x: The Repetti discontinuity, at about 700–1,000 km, separates the upper and lower mantle.
2.tq: one-liner

2.s: Who discovered the discontinuity between the crust and the mantle in 1909?
2.x: The Croatian Andrija Mohorovicic found the Moho in 1909.

2.s: The Indian plate beneath Tibet has been reported to undergo which process?
o: Subduction of its entire crust into the outer core
Complete melting of its oceanic crust at the surface
Delamination of its dense lower layer into the mantle at about 100 km depth
Separation of its upper layer into the asthenosphere only
2.x: The dense lower layer of the Indian plate is reported to be peeling away and delaminating into the mantle at roughly 100 km depth beneath Tibet.
2.tq: Use the process-location-depth combination to distinguish delamination from subduction.
xs: The Indian plate beneath Tibet is **delaminating** — its dense lower layer peeling into the mantle **~100 km** down — option **(3)**.
Evidence: **94 seismic stations** and **helium isotopes**.
xa: The **lithosphere** (about **100 km**) moves over the **semi-fluid asthenosphere**.
The asthenosphere is the **main source of magma**.
Other recent findings: Stanford's first global map of **continental mantle earthquakes**; Swarm data on outer-core flow.

2.s: What is the lithosphere made up of?
2.x: The rigid lithosphere is made of the crust and uppermost mantle, above the weak, ductile asthenosphere.
n: The lithosphere is the rigid upper zone associated with the mantle. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The lithosphere is rigid. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The asthenosphere is weak and ductile. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The lithosphere consists of the crust and uppermost mantle. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The asthenosphere underlies the upper mantle portion below the lithosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: The lithosphere is about **100 km** thick and **broken into tectonic plates**.
Asthenosphere = **low-velocity zone** at ~**100–200 km**.
Lithosphere is an **earthquake-generating shell**; asthenosphere is linked with **mantle flow**.

2.s: Where is the asthenosphere located?
2.x: The asthenosphere is a weak, partly molten upper-mantle zone at about 100–200 km and a major source of magma.
xa: Earthquake waves **slow down** in the asthenosphere; it extends to ~**400 km**.
Lithospheric plates **glide over** it.
**Lithosphere** = crust + rigid uppermost mantle, about **100 km** thick.

2.s: In the sequence Lithosphere – Asthenosphere – Mesosphere – Barysphere, what does the barysphere represent?
2.x: From the surface inward the layers are lithosphere, asthenosphere, mesosphere and barysphere, the last being the core.
xa: **Lithosphere**: crust + rigid uppermost mantle, about **100 km**.
**Asthenosphere**: low-velocity zone at **~100-200 km**; **main source of magma**.
Suess's chemical zones: **SIAL, SIMA, NIFE**.

2.s: Over which weak layer do lithospheric plates glide?
2.x: The weak asthenosphere lets lithospheric plates glide, so mantle movement below can drive them.
n: Mantle movement drives plate movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The asthenosphere allows plate movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Mantle movement drives plate movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: The asthenosphere is the **main source of magma**.
It lies at ~**100–200 km** (extends to ~**400 km**); earthquake waves slow down there.
The lithosphere is the **earthquake-generating shell**.

2.s: Where does magma mainly originate?
2.x: The weak, partly molten asthenosphere is the main source of magma.
2.tq: one-liner

2.s: Apart from Iron and Nickel, which of the following element is an important constituent of inner core of earth?
Which one of the following is present in the largest amount in terms of per cent by mass in the Earth's crust?
2.x: Oxygen is the most abundant element in the Earth's crust by mass, constituting about 46.6% of its total weight. It occurs mainly in combination with other elements, forming oxides and silicate minerals such as silica (SiO₂), alumina (Al₂O₃), and various silicates.

2.s: Which elements are abundant in the formation of interior layer of the earth?
2.x: The elements nickel and ferrum are abundant in the formation of Nife, the inner layer of the Earth. Nife is an abbreviation of Nickel and Ferrum (Iron).

2.s: A chemical element found in abundance in the Earth’s crust is–
2.x: Oxygen is the chemical element found in abundance in the Earth’s crust. The percentage of various chemical elements in Earth’s crust is as follows – (Element) (Percentage by weight) Oxygen (O) - 46.60 Silicon (Si) - 27.72 Aluminium (Al) - 8.13 Iron (Fe) - 5.00 Calcium (Ca) - 3.63 Sodium (Na) - 2.83 Potassium (K) - 2.59 Magnesium (Mg) - 2.09

2.s: Which is the second most abundant element by weight in the Earth's crust?
2.x: Oxygen is the most abundant element by weight in the crust, followed by silicon at about 27.72%.
xa: **Aluminium** is the **most abundant metal**; **iron** second.
⚠ JPSC **2011** keyed **Aluminium** for "second largest".
In the **whole Earth**, **iron** dominates (iron-rich core).

2.s: Which is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust by weight?
2.x: Aluminium (about 8.1%) is the most abundant metal in the crust, followed by iron (about 5%) and calcium (about 3.6%). Silicon (about 27.7%) is more abundant but is not a metal; oxygen is the most abundant element overall.
2.tq: Element order O > Si > Al > Fe; most abundant metal = Al.
xs: **Aluminium** (**8.13%**) is the most abundant **metal** in the crust — option **(2)**.
**Iron** (**5.00%**) is second; **calcium** (**3.63%**) next.
**Silicon** (**27.72%**) is more abundant but not a metal.
xa: **Oxygen** (**46.60%**) is the most abundant element overall.
⚠ JPSC **2011** keyed **Aluminium** for "second largest".
In the **whole Earth**, **iron** dominates.

2.s: Which of the following statements about the composition of Earth’s crust is incorrect?
o: Aluminium constitutes 8.13% by weight and ranks third.
Silicon constitutes 27.72% by weight and ranks second.
Iron constitutes 8.13% by weight and ranks third.
Oxygen constitutes 46.60% by weight and ranks first.
2.x: Option C is incorrect: iron is about 5% and ranks fourth. Aluminium is third at 8.13%, after oxygen (46.60%) and silicon (27.72%).
2.tq: Check the rank and figure of each element.
n: Oxygen constitutes 46.60% of Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Oxygen ranks first among the elements in Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Silicon constitutes 27.72% of Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Silicon ranks second among the elements in Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Aluminium constitutes 8.13% of Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Aluminium ranks third among the elements in Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Iron constitutes 5.00% of Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Iron ranks fourth among the elements in Earth’s crust by weight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xs: The incorrect statement is "**Iron constitutes 8.13% by weight and ranks third**" — option **(3)**: iron is **5.00%** and ranks **fourth**.
**8.13%** and **third rank** belong to **aluminium**.
The others are correct: **oxygen 46.60%** (first), **silicon 27.72%** (second).
xa: Then **calcium 3.63%**, **sodium 2.83%**, **potassium 2.59%**, **magnesium 2.09%**.
**Aluminium** is the **most abundant metal** in the crust; **iron** second.
⚠ JPSC **2011** keyed **Aluminium** for "second largest".
**Whole Earth:** **iron** dominates (core is iron-rich).

2.s: What is SIMA mainly composed of?
2.x: SIMA stands for silica and magnesium (basalt); SIAL is silica and aluminium, NIFE nickel and iron.
2.tq: one-liner

2.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
2.x: NIFE (nickel and iron) forms the core. SIAL is granitic and forms continents; SIMA is basaltic.
2.tq: match

2.s: Oxygen makes up about what percentage of the Earth's crust by weight?
2.x: Oxygen, at 46.60%, is the most abundant element of the crust; silicon is 27.72%, aluminium 8.13% and iron 5%.
2.tq: one-liner

2.s: What does the term ‘NIFE’ refer to?
2.x: NIFE stands for nickel (Ni) and iron (Fe, ferrum), the main metals of Earth's core. N and F would wrongly suggest nitrogen and fluorine.
2.tq: Read the chemical symbols in the acronym.
n: NIFE means nickel and ferrum, or iron. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
xs: **NIFE** stands for **Nickel and Ferrum (iron)** — option **(3)**.
The term comes from **E. Suess**, whose chemical zones were **SIAL**, **SIMA** and **NIFE**; NIFE is the **core** (BPSC **2022**).
The other options wrongly read "N" as **nitrogen** or "F" as **fluorine**.
xa: **Iron** is the core's **main constituent**; **nickel** is **another major constituent**.
**SIAL** = silica + aluminium (granite, continents); **SIMA** = silica + magnesium (basalt, source of magma).
NIFE density ~**11**; it explains Earth's **magnetism**.
Lighter elements in the core: **silicon** (APPSC G2 **2017** answer), sulphur, oxygen.

2.s: Which of the following lighter elements is found in the Earth's core besides iron and nickel?
2.x: Besides iron and nickel, the core holds lighter elements such as silicon, sulphur and oxygen, not aluminium, sodium or potassium.

2.s:
Consider the following statements about the Earth's core:
1. It is made mainly of iron and nickel.
2. Aluminium is one of its important lighter elements.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
2.x: The core is mainly iron and nickel; its lighter elements are silicon, sulphur and oxygen, not aluminium.

2.s: Who gave the terms SIAL, SIMA and NIFE for the layers of the Earth?
2.x: SIAL, SIMA and NIFE are the terms of Suess for the layers by their main elements.

2.s: In the structure of planet Earth, below the mantle, the core is mainly made up of which one of the following?
2.x: Earth's core is composed mainly of iron and nickel (NiFe).

2.s: In the structure of planet Earth, below the mantle, the core is mainly made up of which one of the following ?
2.x: There is an outer core and inner core below the mantle in the structure of the Earth. The outer core is about 2260 km thick (radius) and mostly composed of liquid iron and nickel. The inner core is a hot dense ball of (mostly) iron. It has a radius of about 1220 km.

2.s: The magnetic axis of the Earth is inclined by approximately how much to its geographic axis?
2.x: The Earth's magnetic axis is inclined approximately 11.5° to its geographic axis.
2.tq: Distinguish magnetic-axis inclination from the better-known seasonal axial tilt.
xs: The magnetic axis is inclined **~11.5°** to the geographic axis — option **(2)**.
The field is made by **convecting molten iron** in the **outer core** (geodynamo).
xa: Iron accounts for Earth's **magnetism and rigidity**.
Swarm (**ESA**): outer-core flow under the Pacific switched from **westward** to **eastward**, weakening around **2020**.
Magnetic reversals last up to **~70,000 years**.

2.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the general variation of temperature, pressure and density inside the Earth?
o: Temperature increases, but pressure and density decrease with depth.
Temperature, pressure and density generally increase with depth.
2.x: Temperature, pressure and density all generally rise with increasing depth inside the Earth.
2.tq: Identify the common direction of the three internal gradients.
xs: **Temperature, pressure and density all rise with depth** — option **(2)**.
Pressure rises with the **weight of overlying rock**.
Density goes **2.8-3.0 (crust) → 4.6 (mantle) → 11-13.6 (core)**.
xa: Temperature rises ~**1°C per 32 m** in the upper crust; the rate slows deeper.
Pressure keeps the **inner core solid**.
India's geothermal wells must reach **2-5 km**.

2.s: What is the approximate geothermal gradient in the upper crust?
2.x: Temperature rises by approximately 1°C for every 32 m of depth in the upper crust, although the rate slows at greater depths.
2.tq: Pay attention to the place value in the depth-temperature relationship.
xs: In the upper crust temperature rises ~**1°C per 32 m** — option **(1)**.
The rate **slows deeper**.
xa: **Temperature, pressure and density** all rise with depth.
Highest geothermal potential: **Puga Valley** (**Ladakh**).
Other sites: **Manikaran** (HP), **Tattapani** (Chhattisgarh), **Cambay** (Gujarat), **Bakreshwar** (WB).

2.s: Why is the magnetic field generated by the Earth's liquid outer core important for life?
o: Shields life from solar wind and cosmic radiation
2.x: The magnetic field generated by the liquid outer core helps shield life from the solar wind and cosmic radiation.
xa: The magnetic axis is inclined **~11.5°** to the geographic axis.
Magnetic **reversals** can last up to **~70,000 years**.
**Swarm (ESA)**: outer-core flow under the Pacific switched from sluggish **westward** to strong **eastward**, weakening around **2020**.

2.s: In which State is the Bakreshwar geothermal site located?
2.x: Bakreshwar is in West Bengal; Cambay is the geothermal site of Gujarat, Manikaran of Himachal Pradesh and Tattapani of Chhattisgarh.

2.s: In which layer does convection of conducting material generate the Earth's magnetic field?
2.x: Convection in the liquid outer core generates the field, and changes in that flow are linked to field reversals.
n: Movement and convection of conducting material in the liquid outer core produce the geodynamo. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The geodynamo generates Earth’s magnetic field. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Magnetic-field reversals are linked to changes in molten-core movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: The **magnetic axis** is inclined **~11.5°** to the geographic axis.
**Swarm (ESA):** outer-core flow under the Pacific switched from **westward** to **eastward**, weakening around **2020**.
Magnetic reversals have lasted up to ~**70,000 years**.

2.s: What is the approximate average density of the Earth?
2.x: Earth averages about 5.5 g/cm³, the densest planet, with density increasing inward.
n: Earth’s average density is approximately 5.5 g/cm³. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Earth is the densest planet. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Earth’s density generally increases inward. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Heavier materials are concentrated in Earth’s core. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: Density gradient: **2.8–3.0** (crust) → **4.6** (mantle) → **11–13.6** (core).
**Temperature, pressure and density** all **rise with depth**.
Temperature rises ~**1°C per 32 m** in the upper crust.

2.s: Through which of the following do diamonds mainly reach the Earth's crust from the mantle?
2.x: Diamonds formed in the mantle are transported upward to the crust through kimberlite pipes.
2.tq: Match the resource with its geological transport pathway.
xs: Diamonds reach the crust through **kimberlite pipes** — option **(1)**.
They **form in the mantle**.
xa: **Madhya Pradesh** has **~90%** of India's reserves.
Mantle: Moho to **2,900 km**, silicates rich in **iron and magnesium**.
Mantle: **83%** of volume.

2.s: Which State is associated with approximately 90% of India's diamond reserves?
2.x: Madhya Pradesh is associated with approximately 90% of India's diamond reserves.
2.tq: Link the percentage resource fact with the correct State rather than a geothermal location.
xs: **Madhya Pradesh** has **~90%** of India's diamond reserves — option **(2)**.
Diamonds form in the **mantle** and reach the crust via **kimberlite pipes**.
xa: **Puga Valley** (Ladakh) has the highest **geothermal** potential.
**Bakreshwar** (WB) and **Cambay** (Gujarat) are geothermal sites.
The liquid outer core's field shields life from **solar wind**.

2.s: Where is the Puga Valley geothermal field located?
2.x: Puga Valley in Ladakh is India's highest geothermal field.

2.s: Which ESA mission found that the outer-core flow under the Pacific switched from westward to eastward?
2.x: ESA's Swarm satellites showed the outer-core flow under the Pacific switched direction, weakening around 2020.

Match the following:

2.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Iron is the main constituent of the core.
Nickel is another major constituent of the core.
2.x: Option B is incorrect: the outer core is liquid, which is why S-waves stop there. The inner core is solid and the core is mainly iron and nickel.
2.tq: Discriminate the state of each layer.
n: The outer core is liquid. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The inner core is solid. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The main constituent of the core is iron. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Nickel is another major constituent of the core. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xs: The incorrect statement is "**The outer core is solid**" — option **(2)**: the outer core is **liquid**, so **S-waves stop** there.
The other statements are correct: **iron** is the **main constituent**, **nickel** another major one, and the **inner core is solid**.
xa: The inner core is called the **NIFE** or **solid core**; density **13.3–13.6**.
**Pressure** keeps the inner core solid despite the heat.
⚠ Outer core **liquid**, inner core **solid**.
The core begins at about **2,900 km** depth.

3.s: Which is the second-most abundant element in the Earth's crust by weight?
3.x: Silicon ranks second at about 27.7%; iron is the second-most abundant metal (~5.0%).
xa: Ranks 5–7: **Calcium 3.6**, **Sodium 2.8**, **Potassium 2.6**.
⚠ For the whole Earth, **magnesium (13.9%)** ranks fourth after iron, oxygen and silicon.

3.s:
Consider the following statements about the composition of the Earth as a whole by mass:
1. Iron is the most abundant element.
2. Oxygen is more abundant than silicon.
3. Magnesium is more abundant than silicon.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
3.x: For the whole Earth the order is iron 32.1% > oxygen 30.1% > silicon 15.1% > magnesium 13.9%, so statement 3 is wrong.

3.s: In Suess's classification, what is the granitic continental layer of silicon and aluminium called?
3.x: SIAL (silicon-aluminium) is granitic and continental; SIMA is basaltic and NIFE the nickel-iron core.
xa: These are **Suess's chemical layers** of the Earth.
The crust's most abundant element is **oxygen (46.6%)**; the whole Earth's is **iron (32.1%)**.

3.s: Which is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust?
3.x: Aluminium (8.1%) is the most abundant metal in the crust; iron (5.0%) is second. Iron leads only for the whole Earth.

3.s: Which is the second-most abundant metal in the Earth's crust?
3.x: Iron, at 5.0% by weight, is the second-most abundant metal after aluminium (8.1%).

3.s: In Suess's classification, what does NIFE refer to?
3.x: NIFE is the nickel-iron core; SIAL is the granitic continental layer and SIMA the basaltic layer.

3.s: The idea of weathering is related to-
o: A natural phenomena that breaks rocks into fine
3.x: Weathering is a term which describes the general process by which rocks are broken down at the Earth’s surface into such things as sediments, clays, soils and substances that are dissolved in water. The process of weathering typically begins when the earth’s crust is uplifted by tectonic forces. After the physical breakup and chemical decay of exposed rocks by weathering, the loosened rock fragments and alterations products are carried away through the process of erosion.

3.s: Coal is an example of –
3.x: Sedimentary rocks are formed by the deposition of sediment usually in the form of layers. Sedimentary rocks are also known as layered rocks. Most fossils and mineral oil are found in these rocks. Sedimentary rocks cover 75% of the Earth's surface. Minerals like Coal, Slate, Limestone, Salt, Petroleum, Marble, etc. are examples of sedimentary Rock. Depending on the amount of carbon and hardness, coal is Segregated in to four categories – (i) Anthracite : It is the best kind of coal. It has about 90-95% carbon content. (ii) Bituminous : It is the second most important type of coal and is the most abundant coal. It has a carbon content between 70-90%. (iii) Lignite: It is often referred to brown coal. It has a carbon content between 45-50%. It is mostly used in thermal power stations. (iv) Peat : It is the lowest rank of coal having a carbon content of less than 40%.

3.s: What is Marble?
3.x: Marble is a metamorphic rock that is formed when limestone is subjected to heat and pressure of metamorphism.

3.s: Origin of Metamorphic rocks occurs from …….. rock ?
3.x: "Metamorphism" is a Greek word which means "change of form". Metamorphic rock is a rock that has changed from one type of rock into another. As a result of intense heat from magma and pressure from tectonic shifting, these metamorphic rocks are produced from either igneous rocks or sedimentary rocks.

3.s: Which one of the following is not associated with the 'group'?
3.x: In the given options Limestone, Sandstone and Shale belong to sedimentary rocks, while Gneiss is an example of metamorphic rock. Normally Gneiss is formed from granite.

3.s: Which one of the following groups consists entirely of sedimentary rocks?
3.x: Sandstone, limestone, shale and conglomerate are sedimentary rocks. The other groups contain igneous or metamorphic rocks.
3.tq: Classify every option by identifying the rock type of each member.
xs: **Sandstone, limestone, shale and conglomerate** are all sedimentary — option **(1)** is correct.
Option (2) — **granite, basalt, gabbro, dolerite** — are all **igneous**.
Option (3) — **marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss** — are all **metamorphic**.
Option (4) mixes igneous (granite, basalt), sedimentary (sandstone) and metamorphic (marble).
xa: Other sedimentary rocks: **coal** and **chalk**; **coal** is sedimentary (organic).
Igneous also includes **pegmatite**; metamorphic also includes **schist**.

3.s: Carbon dioxide dissolved in rainwater helps weathering by forming which of the following?
3.x: Carbon dioxide in rainwater forms carbonic acid, which helps weather rocks.
3.tq: Test the chemical agent involved in carbon cycling and weathering.
xs: CO2 in rain forms **carbonic acid**, which weathers rock — option **(1)** is correct.
The carbon ends up stored as **bicarbonate/limestone**.
xa: **Enhanced rock weathering**: crushed fast-weathering **basalt** on farmland locks up CO2 as **bicarbonate**.
Glacier-crushed **pyrite** in the upper **Indus** basin releases CO2 about **three times** faster than silicate weathering removes it.

3.s: What is the branch of geology that studies rocks called?
3.x: Petrology is the study of rocks; it recognises three types – igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic.

3.s: Granite is a/an:
3.x: Granite is a coarse-grained plutonic rock that solidifies slowly beneath the Earth's surface, making it intrusive.

3.s: Which of the following rocks is not likely to contain fossils?
3.x: Among the given options, granite does not contain fossils. Granite is formed from magma from a volcanic eruption. It is an example of Plutonic or Intrusive rocks. Conglomerate, sandstone and shale are examples of sedimentary rocks. Sedimentary rocks contain fossils.

3.s: Which statement of the following is true for igneous rocks?
o: They are both crystal and non-crystal
3.x: The origin of igneous rocks is mainly related to the process of a volcanic eruption. These types of rocks are formed by the cooling and solidification of material called magma or lava. Igneous rocks have both, crystalline and non-crystalline structures and thus the statement given in option (c) is true but all other given statements are wrong because these rocks are composed of silicate minerals and fossils and layers are not found in these types of rocks. Additionally water supply through igneous rocks is very low.

3.s: Which type of rock is formed from cooling and solidification of lava ?
3.x: Igneous rocks are formed by the cooling and solidification of magma/lava. Igneous rocks are of two types: intrusive and extrusive.

3.s: Which of the following is a coarse-grained intrusive igneous rock?
3.x: Intrusive rocks cool slowly at depth, forming coarse grains, as in granite and gabbro.
xa: **Extrusive (volcanic)** lava cools fast at the surface → **fine-grained**: **basalt, rhyolite, andesite**.
APPSC G2 **2024**: **granite = intrusive igneous**.
**Hypabyssal** rocks occur in **dykes and sills** — e.g. **dolerite**.

3.s: Which of the following is a felsic extrusive igneous rock?
3.x: Rhyolite is felsic extrusive; granite is felsic intrusive, diorite intermediate intrusive and basalt mafic extrusive.
xa: **Gabbro** is the **mafic intrusive** counterpart of basalt.
**Andesite** is another extrusive (volcanic) rock.
Volcanic rocks (**andesite, dacite, rhyolite, basalt**) need more energy to fracture than many sedimentary rocks.

3.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Felsic igneous rocks are generally light-coloured and silica-rich.
2. Mafic rocks are always less dense than felsic rocks.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
3.x: Felsic rocks are silica-rich, light-coloured and relatively low in density; mafic rocks, rich in iron, magnesium and calcium, are dark and dense, so statement 2 is wrong.
xa: ⚠ APPSC **2024** Assertion-Reason: "felsic rocks contain high iron, magnesium and calcium" is **false** — that describes **mafic** rocks.
Intrusive examples: felsic = **granite**; intermediate = **diorite**; mafic = **gabbro**.
Mafic minerals include **olivine** and **pyroxene**.

3.s: What are dark, dense igneous rocks rich in iron, magnesium and calcium called?
3.x: Mafic (basic) rocks are rich in Fe, Mg and Ca; felsic rocks are silica-rich and light-coloured.

3.s: Which type of rock is diorite?
3.x: Diorite is intermediate intrusive; rhyolite is felsic extrusive, granite felsic intrusive and basalt mafic extrusive.

3.s:
Consider the following statements made about the sedimentary rocks:
1. Sedimentary rocks are formed at Earth's surface by the hydrological system.
2. The formation of sedimentary rocks involves the weathering of pre-existing rocks.
3. Sedimentary rocks contain fossils.
4. Sedimentary rocks typically occur in layers. Which of these statements are correct?
3.x: Sedimentary rocks are formed at or near the Earth's surface mainly through processes associated with the hydrological cycle, such as weathering, erosion, transportation, deposition, and lithification, making Statement I correct. Their formation involves the breakdown of pre-existing rocks, so Statement II is also correct. These rocks commonly contain fossils because sediments often preserve remains of plants and animals, making Statement III correct. Sedimentary rocks are generally deposited in distinct strata or layers; therefore, Statement IV is also correct.

3.s:
Consider the following statements:
1.

3.s: Sedimentary rocks are called ‘stratified rocks’ because they are generally formed as:
o: Successive layers of deposited, compacted and cemented sediments
Single layers of volcanic ash only
Metamorphosed rocks melted beneath the crust
3.x: Sediments are transported, deposited, compacted and cemented into successive layers called strata.
3.tq: Connect the descriptive term with its formation process.
xs: Sedimentary rocks form as **successive layers** of **deposited, compacted and cemented** sediments — option **(1)** is correct.
These layers are called **strata**, hence **"stratified rocks"**.
Unlayered crystallised magma (option 4) describes **igneous** rock.
xa: The hardening of sediments is called **lithification**.
Sedimentary rocks **may contain fossils** and host **coal, petroleum, natural gas**.

3.s: Which of the following pairs (mode of formation – sedimentary rock) is correctly matched?
3.x: Rock salt is chemically formed; sandstone is mechanically formed and coal organically formed.

3.s: Which of the following describes clay with respect to porosity and permeability?
3.x: Clay has pore spaces, but its very fine particles prevent easy passage of water, so it is porous but impermeable.
xa: **Chalk and sandstone** are both porous and permeable.
**Granite** is neither porous nor permeable.
**Shale / clay** metamorphoses into **slate**.

3.s: Sedimentary rocks cover about what share of the Earth's surface?
3.x: Sedimentary rocks cover about 75% of the Earth's surface and hold most fossils and mineral oil.

3.s: Which rocks are the principal repositories of fossils?
3.x: Sedimentary rocks such as sandstone preserve fossils and hold coal, petroleum and natural gas.
xa: **Archaean** rocks are a **"no fossils"** zone, formed before life.
**Dravidian (Palaeozoic)** rocks are **fossil-rich**, with plenty of marine fossils.

xa: Dravidian age: **600–300 million years**; extra-peninsular.

Archaean = older than **2,500 million years**: granites, gneisses, schists.

3.s: Archaean rocks are fossil-free mainly because they:
o: Are the youngest rocks of India

3.s: Which among the following is connected with Metamorphic rock ?
3.x: Metamorphic rocks are a result of a transformation of existing rock, in a process called metamorphism, which means "change in form". Metamorphic minerals are those that form only at the high temperatures and pressures associated with the process of metamorphism.

3.s: Which one of the following is the odd one out?
3.x: Marble, slate and quartzite are metamorphic rocks, whereas limestone is a sedimentary rock and a parent rock of marble.
3.tq: Identify the common rock class and then locate the parent or non-metamorphic member.
xs: **Limestone** is the odd one out: it is **sedimentary** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Quartzite, marble and slate** are **metamorphic**.
Limestone is the **parent** of **marble**; shale → **slate**; sandstone → **quartzite**.
xa: ⚠ Odd-one-out trap: metamorphic rocks have non-metamorphic parents (**limestone, shale, sandstone, granite**).
**Granite → gneiss**; **coal → graphite** (via anthracite).

3.s: Which of the following is NOT a typical metamorphic mineral?
3.x: Garnet, kyanite and sillimanite are typical metamorphic minerals. Halite is associated with chemically formed sedimentary deposits.
3.tq: Find the odd mineral from a nearby sedimentary category.
xs: **Halite** is NOT a metamorphic mineral — option **(2)** is correct.
Halite is a **chemically formed sedimentary** deposit, like **rock salt** and **gypsum**.
**Garnet, kyanite, sillimanite** (and **staurolite**) are typical metamorphic minerals.
xa: Metamorphic rocks: **marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss, schist**.
Types of metamorphism: **thermal/contact** and **regional/dynamic**.

3.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about rocks?
o: Igneous rocks form by cooling of magma or lava
Granite is extrusive igneous and basalt is intrusive igneous
Metamorphic rocks are existing rocks altered by heat or pressure
Sedimentary rocks form through surface deposition
3.x: It is the reverse: granite is intrusive igneous and basalt is extrusive igneous.
n: Igneous rocks form through cooling or solidification of magma or lava. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Sedimentary rocks form through surface deposition. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Metamorphic rocks form when existing rock is altered by heat or pressure. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Granite is an intrusive igneous rock. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Basalt is an extrusive igneous rock. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: Igneous rocks are "**primary**" rocks (APPSC **2019**) and hold **no fossils**.
**Sedimentary** examples: sandstone, limestone, shale, **coal**; **metamorphic**: marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss.
⚠ **Felsic** (granite) = silica-rich; **mafic** (gabbro) = rich in **iron, magnesium, calcium** (APPSC **2024** trap).
**Deccan Trap** basalt (~**65 million years**) gives **black cotton soil**.

3.s: Which rock is produced by the metamorphism of limestone?
3.x: Limestone becomes marble; shale becomes slate, sandstone quartzite and coal graphite.
xa: **Granite → Gneiss** is the fourth classic pair.
Metamorphism = recrystallisation under **heat and pressure**, without melting.

3.s: What does coal finally become through metamorphism via anthracite?
3.x: Coal is metamorphosed into graphite via anthracite; slate comes from shale.

3.s: Gneiss is usually formed by the metamorphism of which rock?
3.x: Gneiss usually forms from granite; limestone gives marble, sandstone quartzite and shale slate.

3.s: Which metamorphic rock is formed from shale?
3.x: Shale (clay rock) changes into slate under heat and pressure; slate can further become schist.

3.s: Markapur in Andhra Pradesh is famous for which rock industry?
3.x: Markapur in Prakasam district has slate quarries; slate is a metamorphic rock formed from shale.

3.s: Which metamorphic rock is formed from sandstone?
3.x: Sandstone recrystallises under heat and pressure into quartzite, a quartz-rich, non-foliated rock.

3.s: Into which metamorphic rocks does basalt change?
3.x: Metamorphism of basalt gives amphibolite and schist.

2. Statement-II: Rain water contains carbon dioxide in solution.

o: Both Statement-II and Statement-III are correct and both of them explain Statement-I
Both Statement-II and Statement-III are correct, but only one of them explains Statement-I
Only one of the Statements II and III is correct and that explains Statement-I
Neither Statement-II nor Statement-III is correct
3.x: Both Statement-II and Statement-III are correct and both of them explain Statement-I: Rainfall plays a significant role in the weathering of rocks through physical, chemical, and biological processes. As rainwater falls, it absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid, which contributes to the chemical weathering of rocks. Rainwater also contains dissolved gases such as carbon dioxide, nitrogen, and sulphur oxides, which lower its pH to around 5.5 or less, enhancing its corrosive effects. Additionally, dissolved oxygen in rainwater supports oxidation reactions, further promoting chemical weathering of certain rock minerals.

The other examples of metamorphic rocks formed from sedimentary rock are as follows- (1) Shale - Slate (2) Limestone - Marble (3) Chalk and dolomite - Marble (4) Sandstone - Quartzite

3.x: Quartz is silicon dioxide (SiO2), hard and resistant to weathering, and a major component of granite and sandstone.
xa: Quartz is a **tectosilicate** (framework), like **albite** and **orthoclase**.

3.x: Muscovite is a phyllosilicate; albite is a tectosilicate, hornblende a double-chain and augite a single-chain inosilicate.
xa: **Olivine** is a **nesosilicate** (isolated tetrahedra).

3.s: Which of the following pairs (mineral – position in Bowen's reaction series) is correctly matched?
o: Quartz – Crystallises last and is most stable

3.s: Which mineral has a Mohs hardness of 7?
3.x: Quartz has a Mohs hardness of 7. Orthoclase is 6, topaz is 8 and apatite is 5.
3.tq: Use the central value in the hardness scale and distinguish neighbouring entries.
xs: **Quartz** has a Mohs hardness of **7** — option **(4)** is correct.
On the scale, **apatite** is 5, **orthoclase** 6 and **topaz** 8.
xa: The scale runs **1–10**: from **talc** (1) to **diamond (10)**; **corundum** sits just below diamond.
Quartz (**SiO2**) forms a major part of **granite and sandstone** and crystallises **last** in Bowen's series.

3.s: Hornblende belongs to which silicate class?
3.x: Hornblende (amphibole) is a double-chain inosilicate; augite is single chain and mica a phyllosilicate.

3.s: Which of the following pairs (mineral – Mohs hardness) is correctly matched?
3.x: On the Mohs scale topaz is 8; apatite is 5, orthoclase 6 and calcite 3.

3.s: Which is the softest mineral on the Mohs scale of hardness?
3.x: The Mohs scale runs from talc (1), the softest, to diamond (10), the hardest.

3.s: To which silicate class does augite (pyroxene) belong?
3.x: Augite, a pyroxene, is a single-chain inosilicate; hornblende is double-chain.

3.s: Feldspars such as albite and orthoclase belong to which silicate class?
3.x: Albite and orthoclase (feldspars) and quartz are framework silicates, called tectosilicates.

3.s: What are the important agents of metamorphism?
3.x: Heat and pressure transform igneous and sedimentary rocks; complete melting is not required and would lead to magma.
xa: **Melting** in the rock cycle produces **magma**, which forms **igneous** rock.
Examples: **limestone → marble**, **sandstone → quartzite**, **granite → gneiss**.

3.s: Enhanced rock weathering, which locks up carbon dioxide as bicarbonate, involves spreading which crushed rock on farmland?
3.x: Enhanced rock weathering spreads crushed fast-weathering basalt on farmland, where weathering locks carbon dioxide as bicarbonate.
xa: Rain CO2 forms **carbonic acid**, which weathers rock; carbon is stored as **bicarbonate/limestone**.
Glacier-crushed **pyrite** in the upper **Indus** basin releases CO2 about **three times** faster than silicate weathering removes it.

3.s: In the rock cycle, through which process do deposited sediments become sedimentary rock?
3.x: After weathering, erosion and deposition, lithification forms sedimentary rocks; heat and pressure then form metamorphic rocks and melting forms magma.
xa: Full cycle: **Magma → igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic → magma**.
**Key rule:** any rock type can turn into any other.
Sedimentary rock forms through **burial, compaction, cementation**.

3.s: In the rock cycle, what can exposed metamorphic rocks weather into?
3.x: Exposed metamorphic rocks can weather into sediment; any rock type can be transformed into another.
xa: Mantle link: rock material comes up in **eruptions**; **subducted crust** melts back into the mantle.
Cycle: **Magma → igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic → magma**.

Its magnetic field and seismic waves

3.x: Quartzite is a hard, non-foliated metamorphic rock formed when quartz-rich sandstone undergoes recrystallization under intense heat and pressure.

3.s: The black cotton soil of India has been formed due to the weathering of
3.x: The parent rock of black cotton soil is fissure volcanic rock, which consists of igneous rocks formed from the cooling and solidification of lava that erupted through fissures (cracks) in the Earth's crust. These soils are black in colour and are also known as regur soils. Black soil is ideal for growing cotton and is also known as black cotton soil. This type of soil is typical of the Deccan trap (Basalt) region, which spans the northwest Deccan plateau and consists of lava flows. They cover the plateaus of Maharashtra, Saurashtra, Malwa, Madhya Pradesh, and Chhattisgarh, and extend southeast along the Godavari and Krishna valleys. The black soils are composed of extremely fine, i.e., clayey material. They are well known for their ability to retain moisture. In addition, they are rich in soil nutrients, such as calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime. These soils Indian Geography PMF IAS Geo – 98 are generally low in phosphorus. They develop deep cracks during hot weather, which helps with proper soil aeration.

3.s: Quartzite is metamorphosed from :

3.s: Which is the oldest basin in Andhra Pradesh?
3.x:
The Kadapa Basin (Cuddapah Basin) is the oldest geological basin in Andhra Pradesh and one of the oldest sedimentary basins in India. It was formed during the Proterozoic Era, approximately 1.6 billion years ago, and consists of thick sequences of sedimentary and metamorphic rocks. The basin occupies large parts of YSR Kadapa, Nandyal, Kurnool, Annamayya and Prakasam districts. The Kadapa Basin is economically important because it contains rich deposits of limestone, barytes, asbestos, dolomite, quartz and uranium. The famous Mangampeta Barytes Mine, one of the largest barytes deposits in the world, is located within this basin. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).

• Geological Age – Proterozoic
• Famous Mineral – Barytes (Mangampeta)

4.s: The theory that states "pieces of the Earth's crust are in constant, slow motion driven by movement in the mantle" is called:

4.s:
Which of the following are the evidence of the phenomenon of continental drift?
I. The belt of ancient rocks from Brazil coast matches with those from Western Africa.
II. The gold deposits of Ghana are derived from the Brazil plateau when the two continents lay side by side.
III. The Gondwana system of sediments from India is known to have its counterparts in six different landmasses of the Southern Hemisphere.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
4.x: Radiometric dating has shown that both the eastern coast of Brazil and the coastal belt of West Africa contain a strip of very ancient rocks about 2,000 million years old, of the same age and similar nature. The relationship between Ghana’s gold deposits and the source rocks of the Brazilian Plateau is also considered a classic piece of evidence for continental drift. The Gondwana sequence, based on sedimentary rocks derived from glacial deposits, is found across several continents of the Southern Hemisphere, including India, in almost the same thickness, composition, and order. This indicates that these landmasses were once parts of a single supercontinent, Gondwanaland. Therefore, all three statements I, II and III are correct, and the correct option is (c).

4.s: Gondwana-type tillites in India and their counterparts in southern continents support continental drift. What do tillites indicate?
4.x: Tillites are glacial deposits. Their distribution across India and other southern continents indicates that these areas were formerly connected and experienced common glacial conditions.
4.tq: Identify the process represented by a geological deposit.
xs: **Tillites** are **glacial deposits**, so they indicate **ancient glacial conditions** — option **(1)** is correct.
India's **Gondwana-type tillites** have counterparts in the **other southern continents**, showing they were once joined.
xa: Other evidences: **jig-saw fit**, **same-age rocks**, **placer deposits**, **fossils** (Mesosaurus, Glossopteris).
India belonged to **Gondwanaland**, not Laurasia.

4.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Placer deposits — Ghana and Brazil source region
Same-age rocks — Brazil and Western Africa
Jigsaw fit — South America and Africa coastlines

4.tq: Find the incorrectly paired evidence and geographical occurrence.
xs: **Mesosaurus — India and Australia only** is wrongly matched — option **(1)** is correct.
**Mesosaurus** is found in **South Africa and Brazil**.
The other pairs are right: **placer gold** (Ghana, source in Brazil), **same-age rocks** (Brazil–Western Africa), **jig-saw fit** (South America–Africa).
xa: **Lemurs** in **India, Madagascar, Africa** gave rise to the idea of "**Lemuria**".
**Glossopteris** flora is another fossil evidence.

4.s: The ancient rock belts of about 2,000 million years on the Brazil coast match belts found in which region?
4.x: Ancient rock belts on the Brazil coast match rock belts of the same age in Western Africa.
4.tq: Connect the numerical age with the correct matching region.
xs: The **2,000-million-year** rock belts of the **Brazil coast** match those of **Western Africa** — option **(1)** is correct.
This is the "**rocks of the same age** across oceans" evidence (UPSC **2025**).
xa: **Placer gold** of the **Ghana coast** has its source in the **Brazil plateau** (UPSC **2025**).
UPSC **2025** counted rock belts, placer gold and a third evidence as **all correct**.
**Bullard's 1964** computer fit matched South America and Africa.

4.s: The process that continually adds new crust is:
4.x: The process that continually adds new crust is seafloor spreading. Significantly, new crust is created by seafloor spreading. Old crust is destroyed by subduction. It is important to mention here that the two factors roughly balance each other. So the shape and diameter of the Earth remain unchanged. Spreading seafloors are only an aspect of plate tectonics, another is subduction.

4.s: The direct observation of sea-floor spreading in bursts was associated with which conclusion?
o: Sea-floor spreading occurs only at continental interiors.

Sea-floor spreading always occurs at a constant rate.

4.x: The observed rapid episode of sinking, spreading and lava emplacement suggested that sea-floor spreading can occur in bursts rather than at a uniform rate.

xs: The first direct in-situ observation showed **sea-floor spreading happens in bursts** — option **(2)** is correct.
The seafloor sank **4 m**, spread over **1 m**, with **160 million cubic metres** of lava in **16 days**.
xa: **Harry Hess (1961)**: magma rises at **mid-oceanic ridges** and new crust spreads sideways.
Crust age, density and thickness **increase with distance from the ridge** (APPSC **2019**).

4.s: Moving away from a mid-ocean ridge, which one of the following trends is observed in oceanic crust and its sediment cover?
o: Age increases, while density and thickness decrease.
Only sediment thickness increases; crustal age and density remain unchanged.

4.x: The age, density and thickness of oceanic crust, along with the thickness of its sediment cover, increase with distance from the ridge.
